sections.text:
A man sits down to write to a friend. Many have already tried to set the story in order, and he has traced everything accurately from the first, so that Theophilus may know the certainty of what he was taught. That is how Luke begins, as a careful account of the life of Jesus.

It opens with the births of John the Baptist and Jesus, and with songs of praise still used in worship. Then Jesus sets his face toward Jerusalem, and much of the book is that long journey, filled with teaching. Along the road Luke shows special interest in the poor, in women, in outsiders and in prayer. Some of the best-known parables are found only here, among them the Good Samaritan and the Prodigal Son.

The journey ends in Jerusalem, at the cross and the empty tomb. On the road to Emmaus the risen Jesus walks beside two sad travelers and opens the Scriptures to them. The book closes with his ascension, and the disciples return to Jerusalem with great joy.

Early tradition names the author as Luke, a doctor and companion of Paul. The book is addressed to a man called Theophilus and is the first half of a two-part work that continues in Acts. It is commonly dated to the 70s or 80s; some date it to the early 60s.

Luke says he drew on eyewitnesses and earlier accounts, and most scholars think Mark was one of them. Readers differ on how to hold together Luke's sharp words about wealth with other parts of Scripture. His account has shaped the Christian year more than any other: Christmas, the ascension and Pentecost all rest largely on Luke and Acts.

Luke begins like a careful historian. Many have written about these events, he says, and he has traced everything from the start so that Theophilus can know the certainty of what he was taught.

Then the scene is the temple, in the days of Herod. Zacharias, a priest, and his wife Elizabeth have no children, and both are well along in years. As the people pray outside, an angel appears beside the altar of incense. “Don’t be afraid, Zacharias”, he says, and promises a son named John. Zacharias doubts, and the angel, Gabriel, tells him he will be silent until it happens.

Six months later Gabriel appears to Mary in Nazareth. She will conceive by the Holy Spirit and bear a son named Jesus, who will reign on David’s throne forever. Mary answers, “Behold, the servant of the Lord; let it be done to me according to your word.”

She hurries to Elizabeth and sings the song known as the Magnificat. When John is born, Zacharias writes, “His name is John.” His voice returns, and he prophesies a song of blessing.

Luke is the first part of a two-volume work, followed by Acts. Tradition links it with Luke, a companion of Paul, and says he wrote for readers outside Judea. Luke gives special attention to women, the poor and outsiders. The priestly divisions served in the temple in rotation, and burning incense was an honor that a priest might receive only once. Mary’s song echoes Hannah’s prayer in 1 Samuel 2:1 to 10. The virgin birth is held by most Christians as a doctrine, and a few scholars read it differently.

A decree goes out from Caesar Augustus, and everyone must be counted in their own town. Joseph takes Mary from Nazareth to Bethlehem, the city of David. While they are there she gives birth to her firstborn son, and lays him in a feeding trough, because there is no room for them in the inn.

Nearby, shepherds are keeping watch over their flock at night. An angel stands before them, and they are terrified. “Don’t be afraid, for behold, I bring you good news of great joy which will be to all the people.” A Savior has been born, who is Christ the Lord, and the sign is a baby in a feeding trough. Then a multitude of angels praises God. The shepherds hurry to Bethlehem, find the child, and tell everyone. Mary keeps it all in her heart.

At eight days he is named Jesus. In the temple, Simeon and the prophet Anna recognize him, and Simeon tells Mary that a sword will pierce her own soul. When Jesus is twelve, his family finds him after three days in the temple, among the teachers, listening and asking questions.

Luke places the birth within world events and names Roman rulers. Quirinius and the date of the census are debated by historians, and scholars have proposed several ways to line up Luke’s account with other sources. Shepherds were ordinary working people, often of low standing. The offering of two birds in verse 24 was the allowance for families who could not afford a lamb, according to Leviticus 12:8. Simeon’s song is traditionally called the Nunc Dimittis. Passover pilgrimage was a yearly custom for devout families.

Luke pins the moment to the map. It is the fifteenth year of Tiberius Caesar, with Pilate governing Judea, when the word of God comes to John in the wilderness. He goes through the region around the Jordan preaching a baptism of repentance, and Luke recalls Isaiah: “The voice of one crying in the wilderness”.

The crowds come, and John is blunt. Do not lean on being children of Abraham, for the ax already lies at the root of the trees. When people ask what to do, he answers plainly. Share your coats and your food. To tax collectors he says, “Collect no more than that which is appointed to you.” When people wonder if he is the Christ, he says one more powerful is coming, who will baptize with the Holy Spirit and fire. Herod, rebuked for his marriage, shuts John in prison.

Jesus is baptized and praying when the sky opens, the Spirit descends like a dove, and a voice speaks. Then Luke lists Jesus’s family line, back through David and Abraham to Adam.

Tiberius became emperor in the year 14, so the fifteenth year of his reign is usually dated to about 28 or 29. John’s baptism was a washing that marked repentance, and it differs from later Christian baptism. Luke’s family line runs backward and ends at Adam, the son of God, while Matthew’s runs forward from Abraham and differs in several names. Scholars and churches explain the differences in more than one way, for example as two lines of descent or as tracing Mary’s side. Compare Matthew 1.

Led by the Spirit into the wilderness, Jesus fasts for forty days and is tempted by the devil. He is told to turn stone into bread, to worship the devil in return for all the kingdoms, and to throw himself from the temple. Each time Jesus answers with a line from Scripture.

He returns to Galilee and goes to the synagogue in Nazareth, where he reads from Isaiah about good news for the poor and release for captives. He says, “Today, this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing.” The crowd is first impressed, then angry when he points to Elijah and Elisha helping foreigners. They drive him out and try to throw him off a cliff, but he walks away.

In Capernaum he casts an unclean spirit out of a man, heals Simon’s mother-in-law and many others, and says he must preach to other towns too.

The forty days recall Israel’s forty years in the wilderness, and Jesus answers with lines from Deuteronomy 8:3, 6:13 and 6:16. The passage he reads is Isaiah 61:1 and 2, with a phrase from Isaiah 58:6, and the acceptable year of the Lord points to the jubilee year in Leviticus 25. Synagogues were local places for Scripture reading and teaching on the Sabbath. The Gospels differ on the order of the temptations; compare Matthew 4. Christians understand the devil’s role in the story in a range of ways.

Jesus teaches the crowd from Simon’s boat, then tells Simon to let down his nets. After a night of catching nothing, they take in so many fish that the nets begin to break. Simon Peter falls at Jesus’s knees and says he is a sinful man, and Jesus tells him he will now catch people. Simon, James and John leave everything and follow him.

Jesus touches and cleanses a man with leprosy, and heals a paralyzed man whose friends lowered him through a roof. Jesus first says the man’s sins are forgiven, which makes the scribes and Pharisees object, and then tells him to rise and walk.

He calls the tax collector Levi, who gives a feast. When the Pharisees complain about eating with sinners, Jesus says he came to call sinners to repentance. He is asked about fasting and answers with images of a bridegroom, a patch and wineskins.

The lake of Gennesaret is another name for the Sea of Galilee. Leprosy in the Bible covers several skin conditions, and the law in Leviticus 13 and 14 required people with it to live apart until a priest declared them clean. By touching the man, Jesus crosses a boundary. Tax collectors worked for Rome and were often seen as dishonest collaborators, which is why eating with them caused offense. Levi is usually identified with Matthew. The roofs of the time were often flat with a stairway outside.

On a Sabbath, the disciples pick grain and Pharisees object. Jesus reminds them of David eating the consecrated bread and says the Son of Man is lord of the Sabbath. On another Sabbath he heals a man’s withered hand, asking whether it is lawful to do good or harm on the Sabbath. His opponents are furious.

After a night of prayer, Jesus chooses twelve apostles and teaches a large crowd on a level place. He gives blessings for the poor, the hungry and those who weep, and matching woes for the rich and those who are well fed. He then teaches love for enemies, giving to those who ask, and the rule to treat others as you want to be treated, and mercy as the Father is merciful.

He warns against judging, speaks of a speck and a beam, a tree and its fruit, and ends with two builders, one on rock and one without a foundation.

This chapter has a counterpart in the Sermon on the Mount in Matthew 5 to 7. Luke’s version is shorter, and it is set on a level place. The Sabbath rest was a core mark of Jewish identity, and debates about what counted as work were common among teachers. The story of David is in 1 Samuel 21:1 to 6. The twelve apostles recall the twelve tribes of Israel. Christians differ on whether sayings such as offering the other cheek call for non-resistance in every case, and the text gives no guidance for situations of abuse.

In Capernaum a Roman centurion asks Jesus, through Jewish elders and then friends, to heal his dying servant. He says he is not worthy to have Jesus under his roof and that Jesus need only say the word. Jesus is amazed and says he has not found such faith in Israel, and the servant is well.

In Nain, Jesus meets a funeral procession for a widow’s only son, has compassion on her, and tells the young man to arise. The crowd says God has visited his people.

John the Baptist, now in prison, sends two disciples to ask if Jesus is the coming one. Jesus points to what they have seen and heard, and then speaks about John, calling him more than a prophet.

At a Pharisee’s house a woman known as a sinner weeps on Jesus’s feet, wipes them with her hair and anoints them. Jesus tells a parable of two debtors and tells her that her sins are forgiven.

A centurion commanded about a hundred soldiers in the Roman army, and this one is described as a friend to the Jewish community. Luke often highlights outsiders who respond with faith. Nain was a small town near Nazareth. In verse 28 the saying that the least in the Kingdom is greater than John is read in different ways. The woman is not named here, and the text does not say what her sin was. Later tradition sometimes linked her with Mary Magdalene, but the Gospel does not. Compare Isaiah 35:5 and 6 and 61:1.

Jesus travels through towns preaching, with the twelve and with several women who support him from their own means, including Mary Magdalene, Joanna and Susanna. He tells the parable of the sower and explains it: the seed is the word of God, and the soils are different ways of hearing it. He speaks of a lamp that should be seen, and says his mother and brothers are those who hear and do God’s word.

Crossing the lake, Jesus calms a storm. In the country of the Gadarenes he frees a man controlled by many demons. The man is later found clothed and in his right mind. The demons enter a herd of pigs that rush into the lake, and the local people ask Jesus to leave.

Back across the lake, Jairus asks Jesus to heal his dying daughter. On the way, a woman with a twelve-year bleeding is healed by touching his cloak. Jesus then raises Jairus’s daughter.

Luke names women among Jesus’s supporters, which was unusual and shows their role in his ministry. Luke’s account of the parables, the storm and the Gadarene man closely parallels Mark 4 and 5. The abyss in verse 31 is a place of confinement for spirits in Jewish thought. Pigs were unclean animals for Jews, and the herd tells the reader that this was largely non-Jewish territory. Verse 10 draws on Isaiah 6:9 and 10, and Christians read it in different ways.

Jesus sends out the twelve with power over demons and disease, telling them to take nothing for the journey. Herod hears about Jesus and wonders who he is. The apostles return, and Jesus feeds about five thousand with five loaves and two fish.

Peter answers that Jesus is “The Christ of God.” Jesus says the Son of Man must suffer, be rejected, killed and raised, and that followers must take up their cross daily. About eight days later he goes up a mountain to pray with Peter, John and James. His face changes, Moses and Elijah speak with him about his departure, and a voice from the cloud says, “This is my beloved Son. Listen to him!”

He heals a boy the disciples could not heal, and again speaks of his coming betrayal. The disciples argue about greatness, and Jesus sets a child beside him. He then sets his face toward Jerusalem, rebukes James and John for wanting to call down fire on a Samaritan village, and speaks of the cost of following him.

The word translated departure in verse 31 is the Greek word exodus, which links Jesus’s coming death to Israel’s escape from Egypt. This is the middle of Luke: from verse 51 a long journey toward Jerusalem begins. Samaritans and Jews had a long history of conflict and mutual distrust, because they worshiped at different places. Elijah called down fire in 2 Kings 1, which is the reference in verse 54. Some manuscripts add words to verses 55 and 56, and many Bibles have a note about this.

Jesus appoints seventy others and sends them in pairs ahead of him to the towns he plans to visit. He tells them to pray for workers, travel light, stay in one house, heal the sick, and announce that God’s Kingdom has come near. He pronounces woes on towns that saw his deeds and did not repent. The seventy return with joy, and Jesus tells them to rejoice that their names are written in heaven.

A lawyer asks what he must do to inherit eternal life. Jesus asks him what the law says, and he names love of God and love of neighbor. When he asks who his neighbor is, Jesus tells the story of a man beaten by robbers. A priest and a Levite pass by, and a Samaritan stops to care for him. Jesus ends by saying, “Go and do likewise.”

At the home of Martha and Mary, Martha is busy serving while Mary sits listening. Jesus tells Martha that Mary has chosen the good part.

The number seventy may recall the seventy elders in Numbers 11 or the seventy nations in Genesis 10, and some manuscripts read seventy-two. The road from Jerusalem to Jericho drops steeply and was known as dangerous. Priests and Levites served in the temple, and a hearer would expect them to help. Samaritans were looked down on by many Jews, which is the point of the story. Verse 19 about serpents and scorpions is read figuratively by many and literally by few. Mary sitting at a teacher’s feet was a place usually kept for male students.

A disciple asks Jesus to teach them to pray, and he gives a short prayer: for God’s name to be honored, the Kingdom to come, daily bread, forgiveness, and deliverance from the evil one. He tells a story of a friend who knocks at midnight and gets bread because of his persistence, and says to keep asking, seeking and knocking. A father gives good gifts to his children, and the heavenly Father gives the Holy Spirit.

When Jesus casts out a mute demon, some say he does it by Beelzebul. He answers that a divided kingdom cannot stand, and that if he casts out demons by God’s finger, the Kingdom has come. He says the sign given to this generation is the sign of Jonah.

At a Pharisee’s table he pronounces woes on Pharisees and lawyers for neglecting justice and the love of God while attending to small details.

This is Luke’s version of what Christians call the Lord’s Prayer; compare Matthew 6:9 to 13. It is shorter than the one in Matthew, and many church traditions add a closing line of praise that does not appear here. Beelzebul was a name connected with a ruler of demons. The sign of Jonah is explained in different ways: Luke ties it to the preaching of Jonah to Nineveh. The woes against Pharisees and lawyers are criticism within Judaism by a Jewish teacher. They have been misused to attack Jews as a people, and that is not what the text says.

With thousands gathered, Jesus tells his disciples to beware of hypocrisy and not to fear those who can only kill the body. God knows each sparrow and counts the hairs on their heads. Those who acknowledge him before others will be acknowledged before God’s angels, and the Holy Spirit will give words when they are brought before authorities.

When a man asks Jesus to settle an inheritance, Jesus warns against greed and tells the story of a rich man who builds bigger barns and dies that night. He tells his disciples not to be anxious about food or clothing, pointing to ravens and lilies, and to seek God’s Kingdom. He tells them to be ready like servants awaiting their master.

He says he came to bring fire and division, even within families, and urges the crowd to read the present time and settle with an opponent before going to court.

The Pharisees were a lay movement known for careful study of the law. Yeast stands here for something small that spreads. Blaspheming the Holy Spirit in verse 10 has been understood in different ways, and the text gives no help for anyone worried about it beyond what it says. The parable of the watchful servants and the thief at night is about readiness, and Christians differ on how it relates to the return of Christ. Verses 51 to 53 describe division and are not a call to break family ties. Gehenna is the valley near Jerusalem used as an image of judgment.

Some people tell Jesus about Galileans killed by Pilate. Jesus says they were not worse sinners than others, and mentions eighteen who died when a tower fell; he says all need to repent. He tells a parable of a fig tree that bears no fruit, and a gardener who asks for one more year.

On a Sabbath he heals a woman who had been bent over for eighteen years. The synagogue leader objects, and Jesus calls his critics hypocrites, since they untie their animals on the Sabbath, and says she is a daughter of Abraham. He gives two short parables of the Kingdom: a mustard seed and yeast.

Asked whether few will be saved, he tells people to strive to enter the narrow door and says people will come from east and west to sit in the Kingdom. Pharisees warn him that Herod wants to kill him. He replies that he must go on to Jerusalem, and he laments over the city.

The two disasters are not known from other sources, though Pilate is described as harsh by other ancient writers. The text rejects the idea that those who suffer must be worse sinners, which is a point worth noting for readers who face loss. The woman’s healing happens in a synagogue, and Jesus’s title for her echoes Abraham. Verse 34 pictures a hen gathering chicks, a gentle image of protection. The final quotation comes from Psalm 118:26. Christians differ on how verses 24 to 30 relate to who will be saved.

On a Sabbath Jesus eats at the house of a leading Pharisee, where a man with swelling in his body stands before him. Jesus asks whether it is lawful to heal on the Sabbath, and when no one answers, he heals the man.

He sees guests choosing the best seats and tells them to take the lowest place, because those who exalt themselves will be humbled. He tells his host to invite the poor, the crippled and the blind, who cannot repay.

He then tells a parable of a great supper. The invited guests all make excuses, so the host sends his servant to bring in the poor and those from the roads, until the house is full.

Turning to the crowds, Jesus speaks of the cost of following him. He talks of hating family and one’s own life, carrying a cross, and counting the cost like a builder or a king. He ends with a saying about salt.

Meals were an important place for status and honor in the ancient world, which is why seating and guest lists matter here. The word disregard in verse 26 translates a Greek word often rendered hate. Most readers take it as strong, deliberate hyperbole meaning that loyalty to Jesus must come first, rather than a command to feel hostility toward family. Christians read the phrase many are called but few are chosen in more than one way. Compare the similar parable in Matthew 22:1 to 14, which differs in details.

Tax collectors and sinners gather to hear Jesus, and the Pharisees and scribes complain that he welcomes them and eats with them. Jesus answers with three stories about lost things.

A shepherd leaves ninety-nine sheep to find one that is lost, and a woman searches her house for a lost coin. Each calls friends to celebrate, and Jesus says there is joy in heaven over one sinner who repents.

In the third story a younger son asks for his share of his father’s property, travels far away and wastes it. When a famine comes he ends up feeding pigs and wanting to eat their food. He decides to go home and ask to be a hired servant. While he is still far off, his father sees him, runs to him and embraces him, and throws a feast.

The older son, who stayed, is angry and refuses to join. His father comes out and tells him, “Son, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours.”

The three parables are told in answer to the complaint in verse 2. The third story is the best known of Jesus’s parables and is often called the parable of the prodigal son, though readers also focus on the father or on the older brother. Feeding pigs would have been the lowest work imaginable for a Jewish listener. The story ends without saying whether the older son goes in, which leaves the question open to the Pharisees who are listening. Compare Ezekiel 34 for the image of God as shepherd.

Jesus tells his disciples about a rich man's manager who is accused of wasting his master's goods. Facing dismissal, the manager reduces what several debtors owe, hoping they will take him in. The master commends his shrewdness. Jesus adds sayings about using worldly wealth, being faithful in little things, and the fact that no one can serve both God and money.

The Pharisees, who love money, scoff. Jesus says God knows their hearts, speaks of the law and the prophets until John, and says it is easier for heaven and earth to pass away than for a stroke of the law to fall. He gives a short saying about divorce.

He then tells of a rich man who lives in luxury and a poor beggar named Lazarus at his gate. After they die, Lazarus is comforted and the rich man is in torment. Abraham says a great gulf is fixed, and that the rich man’s brothers have Moses and the prophets.

The parable of the manager is one of the most debated in the Gospels. Readers differ on whether the master praises the manager’s dishonesty or his foresight, and on what the changes to the bills were. The word mammon is an Aramaic word for wealth. The story of the rich man and Lazarus is told as a parable, and Lazarus is the only person named in any of Jesus’s parables. Hades here is the place of the dead, and Christians differ on how this story relates to teaching about the afterlife and judgment.

Jesus warns that things that make people stumble will come, but woe to those who cause them, especially to little ones. He teaches that a brother who sins should be rebuked, and forgiven if he repents, even seven times in a day. The apostles ask for more faith, and Jesus answers with the picture of a mustard seed, then a short picture of a servant who does his duty.

On the way to Jerusalem, ten men with leprosy call to him from a distance. He tells them to show themselves to the priests, and they are cleansed as they go. Only one, a Samaritan, returns to give thanks, and Jesus tells him his faith has healed him.

Asked when God’s Kingdom will come, Jesus says it does not come with observation. He then speaks to the disciples of the days of the Son of Man, comparing them to the days of Noah and of Lot, and says to remember Lot’s wife.

Showing themselves to the priests followed the law in Leviticus 14 for those who believed they had been healed of a skin disease. A Samaritan was a double outsider, as a foreigner and a member of a group that many Jews avoided. The phrase in verse 21 is translated within you in some Bibles and among you in others, and Christians differ on which is meant. The sayings about the days of the Son of Man are read in different ways, as are the taken and left in verses 34 and 35. Verse 36 is not in the oldest manuscripts, as the text here notes. See Genesis 6 to 7 and 19.

A widow will not stop knocking. The judge in her city fears neither God nor people, and he gives in only because she wears him out. Jesus tells it so that his hearers will always pray and not give up.

Two men go up to the temple to pray. The Pharisee thanks God that he is not like other people. The tax collector stands far off and says, “God, be merciful to me, a sinner!” Jesus says it was this man who went home justified.

Babies are brought to Jesus, and he welcomes them. A rich ruler asks about eternal life, hears that he lacks one thing, and goes away very sad. Jesus tells the twelve about Jerusalem, and they understand none of it. Outside Jericho a blind beggar cries out until Jesus stops, and he sees.

Jesus is on the road to Jerusalem, a journey that Luke has been following since chapter 9. The chapter gathers prayer, pride, wealth and faith into one stretch of road, and each scene is a person who comes to Jesus in need. Several of these scenes appear in Matthew and Mark too, but the two parables of prayer are found only in Luke. The warning about what is coming in Jerusalem sets the shadow of the cross over everything else in the chapter. Readers have long noted how often Luke places the poor and overlooked at the center.

Zacchaeus is rich, a chief tax collector, and he cannot see over the crowd. So he runs ahead and climbs a sycamore tree. Jesus stops under it, looks up and calls him by name: “Zacchaeus, hurry and come down”. The crowd murmurs that Jesus has gone to be the guest of a sinner. Zacchaeus stands and promises to give half of his goods to the poor and to repay four times over anyone he has wronged. Jesus says that salvation has come to this house.

Because the crowd expects the Kingdom at once, Jesus tells of a nobleman who goes away to receive a kingdom and leaves his servants with money to put to work. Then Jesus rides a colt into Jerusalem while his disciples praise God, and he weeps over the city. He drives sellers out of the temple and teaches there daily.

Jericho is the last stop before Jerusalem, and Luke slows down here. Tax collectors were widely resented in Judea, so the crowd's murmuring is easy to understand. The parable of the nobleman is told because people near Jerusalem expected God's Kingdom to appear immediately. Matthew 25 has a related parable, and Christians read the story differently: some see a call to faithful work until Christ returns, while others stress the nobleman's rejection by his own citizens. The scene of the colt and the cloaks is told in all four Gospels; compare Mark 11 and John 12.

The leaders ask Jesus in the temple who gave him his authority. He answers with a question about John's baptism, and they are trapped. If they say it came from heaven, they will be asked why they did not believe. If they say it came from men, the people will stone them. They say they do not know, and Jesus gives no answer either.

He tells of a man who rents out a vineyard. Servant after servant is beaten, and finally the owner sends his beloved son, and the farmers kill him. The leaders understand that the story is aimed at them.

Spies then ask about taxes, and Jesus says to give “to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s.” The Sadducees ask about a woman and seven brothers, and Jesus answers that God is the God of the living.

This is the first of several days of questions in Jerusalem. Each group tries to catch Jesus in public: the chief priests and elders, then spies sent to hand him to the governor, then the Sadducees. The Sadducees did not believe in the resurrection, and this is why their question is built to ridicule it. The vineyard parable echoes the image of Israel as a vineyard in Isaiah 5. Christians have sometimes misused this parable against Jews as a people. The text itself is aimed at particular leaders in Jerusalem, and Jesus himself and his followers were Jews.

Jesus looks up and sees rich people dropping gifts into the temple treasury. Then he sees a poor widow put in two small coins. He says that she has put in more than all of them, because they gave from their abundance and she gave all she had to live on.

Some nearby admire the temple's beautiful stones. Jesus says the day is coming when not one stone will be left on another. They ask when, and his answer is long and sober. Many will come in his name and lead people astray. There will be wars and earthquakes, and his followers will be handed over and hated, yet not a hair of their heads will perish. He speaks of Jerusalem surrounded by armies and of the Son of Man coming in a cloud. He ends with a call to stay watchful, while the people come early each morning to hear him.

The widow's gift is the quiet scene before a loud one. Many scholars think Luke wrote after the Roman destruction of the temple in the year 70, and the words about Jerusalem surrounded by armies are often read in that light. Christians differ on how the chapter fits together: some see the fall of Jerusalem as the main subject, some see the end of the age, and many see both woven together. Compare Mark 13 and Matthew 24. This kind of writing about the end was familiar in Jewish tradition, and it was meant to comfort the faithful as well as to warn.

The Passover is near, the leaders are looking for a way to kill Jesus, and Judas, one of the twelve, goes to them. At the table Jesus says he has earnestly desired to eat this Passover with his friends before he suffers. He breaks the bread, saying “This is my body which is given for you”, and passes the cup of the new covenant. One at the table will betray him, and the disciples argue over who is greatest. He answers that the greatest must be like one who serves.

He tells Peter that he has prayed for him. On the Mount of Olives he prays, “Father, if you are willing, remove this cup from me.” Judas arrives with a crowd and a kiss. Peter denies Jesus three times, the rooster crows, and Peter weeps bitterly.

This is the night before the crucifixion, told in Luke with attention to both friendship and failure. The Passover meal remembered Israel's rescue from Egypt, and Jesus gives it new meaning. Christians differ on how the bread and cup are to be understood, and traditions such as Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran, Reformed and Baptist churches teach different things. Verses 43 and 44, on the angel and the sweat like drops of blood, are missing from some early copies, so some Bibles mark them with a note. The saying about buying a sword is read in several ways, and verse 51 shows Jesus healing, not fighting.

Jesus stands before Pilate, accused of opposing taxes to Caesar and of calling himself a king. Three times Pilate says he finds no basis for a charge. He sends Jesus to Herod, who has long wanted to see a miracle and gets no answers. Back before Pilate, voices rise for Barabbas, a man jailed for revolt and murder, and for Jesus to be crucified. Pilate gives in.

Simon of Cyrene is made to carry the cross. At the place called The Skull, Jesus says, “Father, forgive them, for they don’t know what they are doing.” Rulers and soldiers mock him. One of the criminals beside him asks to be remembered, and Jesus answers, “today you will be with me in Paradise.” Darkness falls over the land, and Jesus commits his spirit to the Father. A centurion calls him a righteous man. Joseph of Arimathaea lays the body in a new tomb, and the women watch.

Luke stresses Jesus' innocence again and again. Pilate, Herod and one of the criminals each say or show that nothing here deserves death. The words forgiving those who crucify him are missing from some early copies, and some Bibles mark verse 34 with a note. This chapter has been used to blame the Jewish people for the death of Jesus, which is a grave misreading. The text names particular leaders and a crowd in Jerusalem, and it also shows Roman authority carrying out the sentence. Compare Mark 15 and John 19.

At dawn on the first day of the week, women come to the tomb with spices and find the stone rolled away and no body inside. Two men in dazzling clothing ask why they seek the living among the dead. The eleven think the women's story is nonsense.

That day two disciples walk to Emmaus, sad and talking. A stranger joins them, and their eyes are kept from knowing him. They tell him of a hope that seemed to have died. He opens the Scriptures to them, beginning with Moses and the prophets. At the table he takes bread and gives thanks, they know him, and he is gone. They say, “Weren’t our hearts burning within us” as he spoke.

They hurry back to Jerusalem, and Jesus stands among the gathered disciples, shows his hands and feet and eats broiled fish. Then he blesses them and is carried up, and they return with great joy.

This is the end of Luke's Gospel, and Acts begins by picking up the same thread; see Acts 1. Luke tells that the first witnesses were women whose word was not believed at first. The chapter is built around the Scriptures: Jesus reads the story of his own suffering back through Moses, the prophets and the psalms. Emmaus is named as sixty stadia from Jerusalem, and its exact site is debated. Christians have long drawn a link between the breaking of bread here and the meal in chapter 22. Compare the resurrection accounts in Matthew 28, Mark 16 and John 20.
